title: AI’s Giant Money Loop Is Drawing Foreign Cash Like 2008
author: Shawn Donnan, Estelle Ou - Economist, and Jorgelina Do Rosario
summary: 全球经常账户失衡回到 2008 年危机前以来最高、接近 150 年峰值：中国出口创纪录顺差，美国财政赤字与 40 万亿美元债务膨胀。新变量是 AI：韩国、台湾等芯片出口国积累的储蓄回流美国，为科技巨头约 9 万亿美元的 AI 建设融资，形成循环资金流，推高美债与主权债收益率，也把 AI 泡沫破裂的风险扩散到亚洲投资者。

paragraphs.text: If you want to understand the way capital is flowing around the world right now and the new stress points forming, take a drive outside Washington to Loudoun County, Virginia. Two decades ago, it was a focal point of a housing boom fanned by a global savings glut that turned horribly wrong. More recently, a new wave of overseas money has poured in to fuel a boom in data center campuses with the power needs of small cities.

The parallel for Loudoun County – and the global economy – has investors and economists asking whether the artificial intelligence boom is being financed in the same unstable way that unraveled in the 2007-08 subprime crisis, and what happens if the promised profits are slow to arrive.

Loudoun County bet heavily on data centers to fill the revenue gap left by collapsing property tax revenues a generation ago. Globally, comparisons between the subprime episode and today’s AI investment boom are being drawn because of the yawning imbalances that underpin both. The gap between surplus savers like China and Japan and deficit economies like the US is back at the highest level since the leadup to the 2007-08 global crisis and is nearing a 150-year peak, a level that has preceded past turmoil.

At the core of that imbalance lie familiar behemoths. China’s ultracompetitive exports are creating record trade surpluses, while America’s gaping fiscal deficit and swelling $40 trillion debt pile are unsettling the bond market. Layered over those is a new and potentially riskier dynamic: an AI boom creating massive demand for high-end chips and new pools of savings in places that make them like South Korea and Taiwan which are flowing to fund American tech companies and their $9 trillion AI build out.

It’s a circular flow of capital that’s contributing to higher yields on US Treasuries and sovereign bonds, raising the cost of servicing debts. Globally, it spreads the risks of an AI bust beyond Silicon Valley to investors in Asia and beyond. And it’s all happening in a world in which superpower rivalries and stressed alliances make the prospects of cooperation in the event of a crisis more difficult.

“We are not in a safe space,” says Beatrice Weder di Mauro, who leads the Paris-based Centre for Economic Policy Research and got the call last year from France’s Élysée Palace requesting a report on the state of global imbalances for this summer’s meeting of Group of Seven leaders.

She sees the growing asymmetry as a collision of a disruptive technological revolution, geopolitical uncertainty and a new wave of protectionism. She also sees building risks, both as the exposure spreads to investors around the world and as a narrow group of “technostates” now benefiting from the AI boom become so dependent on it that she likens it to the Dutch disease usually associated with economies that become distorted by their overreliance on resources.

If projections from the International Monetary Fund hold true, the cumulative increase in excess savings that have built up in the global economy since 2023 will reach $1.95 trillion by the end of 2026, or a third larger than the $1.5 trillion rise over the comparable three-year period in the run-up to the 2008 crisis. In the early 2000s, such excess savings tended to flow from foreign central banks into Treasuries and other US bonds, helping keep US borrowing costs low. A different dynamic is now in play.

Governments today are purchasing fewer Treasuries, with worries over America’s swelling debt and geopolitics two contributing factors. Instead, the savings pools are often in private hands and shifting to a narrow set of other traded assets like corporate stocks and bonds, a significant portion of which are feeding the AI boom. Foreign investors made roughly $1.5 trillion in net purchases of US equities alone since the beginning of 2024 through the end of July.

A Bloomberg Economics analysis of Treasury data shows that in 2025 roughly 20% of all foreign holdings of US equities were in AI-related sectors, up from roughly 10% in 2019. That number has grown with soaring valuations since then. But even assuming that 20% level, foreign investors had about $4.9 trillion of exposure to US-listed shares of companies in industries at the center of the AI boom at the end of June. That’s roughly equivalent to Germany’s annual GDP.

Like portfolio flows, greenfield foreign direct investment in long-term projects like factories and power plants is increasingly concentrated in AI-related projects and other strategic industries. Moreover, thanks to the US’s outsize AI role, the rich world has seen much faster growth in FDI than developing economies, according to United Nations data.

All of which means that even as a world tied to the effects of both real wars and trade wars is seeing investment being held back, the bets that are being made are increasingly tied to an industry facing major questions – from just how AI will change the world to how it will survive a local and national political backlash to the structures used to finance it all. That’s vexing economists at the IMF, who earlier this year warned in a paper that a rapid acceleration in AI adoption that sparks another surge in US business investment could widen the US current account deficit even further.

“From the perspective of the IMF, it has huge implications for capital flows globally,” the IMF’s top US official, First Deputy Managing Director Dan Katz, a former aide to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, said of the AI boom at a Washington event in September. He pointed to potential ramifications, ranging from the performance of markets to growing gaps in growth between the US and other countries.
Why AI Is Sucking Up the World’s Wealth

In an October paper, economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of the Columbia Business School calculated that by 2032 the cumulative investment in AI-related infrastructure would reach nearly $9 trillion, which would see it significantly outstrip the 19th century railroad boom as the largest capital expenditure spree in US history as a share of GDP.

Debts and obligations to finance that are piling up. Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc., Meta Platforms, and Oracle Corp. have collectively agreed to nearly $3 trillion dollars in leases, purchase commitments, and guarantees that don’t show up on the companies’ balance sheets.

Meantime, windfall profits for big chip makers like Taiwan’s TSMC and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics mean they’re sitting on massive cash piles. Samsung’s free cash flow alone is almost a quarter of the value of South Korea’s central bank foreign-exchange reserves.

Just as the flows have changed, so have the main players. Where once a significant share of savings in surplus countries were managed by central banks and invested in US Treasuries, these days they’re controlled by hedge and pension funds with higher appetites for risk and yield. South Korean investors poured a net $17 billion into US equities in 2023; in the 12 months through July this year that figure ballooned to $69 billion.

“Asian capital is the fuel that feeds the US AI boom,” says Frederic Neumann, Chief Asia Economist at HSBC Holdings Plc in Hong Kong. And all of that “sits on top of precarious global imbalances in demand and capital flows,” he adds. “A stumble in AI investments would thus entail painful adjustments, for the US, for the greenback, and for Asia and the world.”

David Chao, global market strategist at Invesco Ltd., which oversees about $2.5 trillion in assets, says the irony is that “the very economies supplying the savings that are funding the AI boom may also be among the biggest casualties if the boom unwinds.” Though Chao also argues the global financial system is less exposed than it was ahead of the 2008 crisis because the investment is fundamentally more productive.
“The technology is real, adoption is real, and many of the leading companies are highly profitable,” he says. “What I worry about is that investor expectations soon may become impossible to meet.”

The Bloomberg Magnificent Seven Index comprising Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla has surged by more than 380% since the start of 2023. Meantime, windfall profits for big chip makers like Taiwan’s TSMC and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics mean they’re sitting on cash piles that rival the foreign exchange reserves at central banks. Samsung’s free cash flow alone is more than six times the value of South Korea’s central bank reserves.

Hung Tran, nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center, likens the resulting reinvestment of surplus in dollars from Taiwan and South Korea to the structural shift in the 1970s and the wealth tied to oil and gas. Much like Middle Eastern oil producers in the past, the new tech powers depend on the US security umbrella and are paid in dollars. “The tech dollars now are a new version of petrodollars,” he says.

Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas, who until earlier this year served as IMF chief economist, argues that in many ways the global economy is working as it should. “If you do have a technological revolution that requires a lot of capital investment” concentrated in a few countries, it’s far more efficient for those countries “to be attracting capital from all over the world to fund that revolution rather than rely on their domestic savings,” he says.
Then again, Gourinchas adds, “even a technological revolution is not a blank check.” And there are already other effects.

In the early 2000s, the surge in net savings in Asia and from energy producers in the Middle East and elsewhere helped bring down interest rates in the US and the rest of the world by flowing into US Treasuries and bonds. This time around, bond yields and interest rates are going up. The result is that the cost of servicing debt mountains in the US and other rich countries is also rising. Which contributes to a worsening fiscal situation and yet more anxiety in bond markets.

One key difference today is the state of public balance sheets. While the tech bubble may have contributed to higher interest rates in the late 1990s, “the debt levels of governments then, relative to output, were a third or half of where they are now,” Gourinchas says. Now, higher rates bite harder and the high cost of servicing debt reduces the fiscal space to respond to a crisis.
To some long-term watchers of global capital flows, it all adds up to a more volatile mix than what we’ve seen before.

Gian Maria Milesi-Ferretti, who in the early 2000s was part of the IMF team monitoring the build up of imbalances that led to the 2007-08 crisis, argues that besides the debt hanging over the rich world, the fundamental issue is the far larger role played by private investors. And it’s not just that international hedge funds and pension funds are betting on AI, it’s that they’re often using holdings of US Treasuries as collateral to do so. Some estimates this year have put hedge funds' holdings of US Treasuries at a record 8% of the $32 trillion market.

In a September paper, Federal Reserve economists pointed to the decline of buying by foreign central banks and the rising role of hedge funds in the Treasuries market as a factor behind rising bond yields. “The declining participation of less price-sensitive foreign official investors, combined with the increasing role of more price-sensitive hedge funds and other private investors, has fundamentally altered market dynamics,” the Fed economists wrote, pointing to the potential of that shift “amplifying the effects of shocks on yields.”

That’s because central banks have traditionally been largely passive owners of US sovereign bonds. But private investors are much more likely to offload Treasuries if they have to cover losses elsewhere, Milesi-Ferretti says. Put simply: The risk today isn’t that China’s central bank or others will offload their US Treasuries, it’s that private investors may.
“These guys move really fast,” Milesi-Ferretti says. “All this, to me, points to a riskier outlook than the one you would've thought about even three, four years ago.”

In Loudoun County today more than 40% of its tax receipts – $1.2 billion in fiscal 2026 – come from data centers through which a significant share of global internet traffic flows, making it uniquely exposed if an AI bubble bursts.

“We would see more impact than some other parts. I mean, it's not even ‘Could we?’ We would,” says Phyllis Randall, chair of the county’s board of supervisors, who points to what is now the local government’s heavy dependence on tax revenues tied to data centers.

Randall argues that because the data centers in Loudoun aren’t the type that host AI training models the county may not be as exposed to an AI bust as some other places. Yet the centers that are there are the very sort that provide the general computing capacity that AI models depend on once they’re operating, she also concedes.

Local officials in September decided to pause approvals for new data centers amid a growing backlash from residents. “We're full,” Randall says. That hasn’t stopped the construction of previously approved data centers, including some backed by foreign capital.

Among those is a campus being built by data center developer and operator Yondr, which in 2025 was bought by Canadian pension fund La Caisse and New York-listed DigitalBridge. The latter in turn last December announced it was being acquired for $4 billion by Japanese tech titan Masayoshi Son’s Softbank. So far, two data centers that draw 96 megawatts of electricity have been completed as part of the project. Eventually the plan is to have a complex that would consume four times that (336 MW), or roughly the power needed to keep the lights on in a city of 750,000 people akin to nearby Washington DC.

If one of the reasons for the backlash in Loudoun County is data centers’ power usage and their impact on residential electricity prices, for local officials the anxiety is increasingly about revenues and the local economy’s dependence on the sector. They’ve started planning for the possibility of an AI bubble bursting, aware of their exposure and what happened in 2007-08.

The county isn’t sitting still. In 2024, it set up a $120 million “revenue stability fund” specifically to make up for any collapse in data center revenues. They’re also drafting a plan for what to do if, or when, the time comes that those data centers shut down either because of a crisis or simple obsolescence, including potentially requiring operators to take out a “decommissioning bond” that would cover the costs.

In the AI boom and the data centers that have proliferated as a result Loudoun County has been the “test case,” says Laura TeKrony, who chairs the transportation and land use committee for the board of supervisors. It doesn’t want to end up as ground zero in a new crisis, she says.

“We know it's coming, so we're trying to diversify our economy,” TeKrony says of a potential slowdown in the AI revenues that now provide more than 40% of the budget. “That's a lot. That's financial risk.”
